final_proof:
Fix the parameter \(p>0\) occurring in the definition of \(\ell^p\), and write
\[
\ell^p=\left\{x=(x_n)_{n\ge 1}\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}:\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|x_n|^p<\infty\right\}.
\]
(Under the usual convention, \(1\le p<\infty\); the proof actually works for every \(p>0\).) Pointwise addition is defined by
\[
(x+y)_n=x_n+y_n.
\]
For \(a\in\mathbb R\), regard \(a\) as the constant sequence \((a,a,\ldots)\). Its pointwise product with \(x\) is the scalar multiple \(a\cdot x\), so
\[
(a\cdot x)_n=ax_n.
\]

We first verify closure. If \(u,v\ge0\), then
\[
(u+v)^p\le 2^p(u^p+v^p),
\]
because \(u+v\le2\max\{u,v\}\), the function \(t\mapsto t^p\) is increasing on \([0,\infty)\), and \(\max\{u,v\}^p\le u^p+v^p\). Thus, if \(x,y\in\ell^p\), the triangle inequality gives, for every \(n\),
\[
|x_n+y_n|^p\le (|x_n|+|y_n|)^p\le2^p(|x_n|^p+|y_n|^p).
\]
Consequently,
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|x_n+y_n|^p
\le2^p\left(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|x_n|^p+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|y_n|^p\right)<\infty.
\]
Here the inequality first holds for finite partial sums and then remains true upon taking their increasing limits. Hence \(x+y\in\ell^p\).

If \(a\in\mathbb R\) and \(x\in\ell^p\), then
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|ax_n|^p
=|a|^p\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|x_n|^p<\infty;
\]
when \(a=0\), both sides are zero. Therefore \(a\cdot x\in\ell^p\). Thus pointwise addition is an internal operation on \(\ell^p\), while pointwise multiplication by constant real sequences defines an external scalar multiplication \(\mathbb R\times\ell^p\to\ell^p\).

It remains to verify the algebraic axioms. Let \(x,y,z\in\ell^p\) and \(a,b\in\mathbb R\). Two sequences are equal precisely when their corresponding coordinates are equal. The field laws in \(\mathbb R\) therefore give, for every \(n\ge1\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
((x+y)+z)_n&=(x_n+y_n)+z_n=x_n+(y_n+z_n)=(x+(y+z))_n,\\
(x+y)_n&=x_n+y_n=y_n+x_n=(y+x)_n,\\
(a\cdot(x+y))_n&=a(x_n+y_n)=ax_n+ay_n=(a\cdot x+a\cdot y)_n,\\
((a+b)\cdot x)_n&=(a+b)x_n=ax_n+bx_n=(a\cdot x+b\cdot x)_n,\\
((ab)\cdot x)_n&=(ab)x_n=a(bx_n)=(a\cdot(b\cdot x))_n,\\
(1\cdot x)_n&=x_n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus addition is associative and commutative, both distributive laws hold, scalar multiplication is compatible with multiplication in \(\mathbb R\), and \(1\) acts as the scalar identity.

Finally, the zero sequence \(0=(0,0,\ldots)\) belongs to \(\ell^p\), since its defining series is zero, and \(x+0=x\) coordinatewise. For each \(x\in\ell^p\), the sequence \(-x=(-x_n)_{n\ge1}\) also belongs to \(\ell^p\), because
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|-x_n|^p=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|x_n|^p<\infty,
\]
and \(x+(-x)=0\) coordinatewise. Hence \((\ell^p,+)\) is an abelian group, and all scalar-multiplication axioms over \(\mathbb R\) hold. Therefore \(\bigl(\ell^p,+,\cdot\bigr)_{\mathbb R}\) is a real vector space.
